Name: ISAs
General structure:
RISC-V -> Embedded realtime systems, warehouse computers
ARMv8/SVE -> Embedded realtime systems, Personal computer, warehouse
Intel x86 -> Personal computer, warehouse

Complex Instruction Set Computers (CISC)
- Many special purpose instructions.
- Example: x86. Now almost 900 instructions.
- Typically various encoding lengths (x86, 1-15 bytes)
- Different number of clock cycles, depending on
instruction.

Reduced Instruction Set Computers (RISC)
- Few, regular instructions. Minimize hardware complexity.
- RISC-V is a good example (ARM mostly RISC)
- Typically fixed instruction lengths (e.g., 4 bytes for RISC-V)
- Typically one clock cycle per instruction (excluding memory
accesses and cache misses)

RISC-V is the focus because
i) it is relatively easy to understand
ii) many text-books on RISC-V,
iii) A lot of research and focus on it

Name: C to asm
General structure:
1. C-code, a=b+c
The compiler maps (if possible) C variables to registers (a->s_0, b->s_1, c->s_2)
2. RISC-V Assembly Code, add s0, s1, s2
The assembly code is a human-readable form of the machine code
3. RISC-V Machine Code, 0x01248433
Each assembly instruction is mapped to one or more machine code instructions.
In RISC-V, most instructions are 32 bits (there is support for compressed instructions, but we will not tackle them in the course).

Name: Memory (latent storage, slow but larger)
General structure:
Has many more data locations than registers, Accessing memory is slower than accessing registers.
A processor’s word size is the data width it can handle in one operation. A 32-bit processor has 32-bit words. A 64-bit processor has 64-bit words.

The choice of endianness is arbitrary, but creates problems when communicating between processors with different endianness.
- Big-endian: the most significant byte (MSB) of the word is stored at the lowest memory address.
- Little-endian: the least significant byte (LSB) is stored at the lowest memory address.

Name: Machine code/Instruction format
General structure:
Where a RISC-V program is stored is dictated by a linker (during compilation). In DTEK-V board, we start code immediately at address 0x0.
In RISC-V, each instruction requires exactly one word (32 bits) of space.
RISC-V code must be word-aligned (start at addresses 0,4, 8, C etc.). X86 does not require word alignment.

R-type (register-type), instructions have three register operands: two sources and one destination
(funct7, 7), (rs2, 5), (rs1, 5), (funct3, 3), (rd, 5), (opcode, 7)
funct3/7: determines the specific R-type operation to perform.
rs1, rs2: source operands 1 and 2
rd: destination op (where is the result saved)

I-type (immediate-type), A few I-Type instructions are encoded slightly differently, but are still considered I-Type. These are shift immediate instructions (srli, slli, srai).
(imm, 12), (rs1, 5), (funct3, 3), (rd, 5), (opcode, 7)
imm: immediate value (signed-extended)
rs1: source operand
funct3: determines the operation to perform
rd: destination op (where is the result saved)

Special I-type (encoded slightly differently, but still considered I-type), srli, slli, srai
(Imm_(11:5), 7), (shamt, 5), (rs1, 5), (funct3, 3), (rd, 5), (opcode: 7)
Since funct3 for srli and srai is the same (101_2), imm11:5 encodes whether its an arithmetic or logical shift.

S-type (store-type), sw
(Imm_(11:5), 7), (rs2, 5), (rs1, 5), (funct3, 3), (Imm_(4:0), 5), (opcode, 7) 
rs1, rs2: source operands 1 and 2
funct3: determines the operation to perform (e.g. the size of the store)
Imm needs to be concatenated to form the immediate value

B-type (branches), beq
(Imm_12, 1), (Imm_(10:5), 6), (rs2, 5), (rs1, 5), (funct3, 3), (Imm_(4:1), 4), (Imm_11, 1), (opcode, 7)
rs1, rs2: source operands 1 and 2
funct3: determines the operation to perform (e.g. the size of the store)
Imm needs to be concatenated to form the immediate value

Conditional branches compute their addresses relative to the program counter (PC) because the instructions have not enough address bits. Calculate branch target address (BTA): BTA = PC + signext(concat(imm_(12:1),'0'))

U-type (lui, auipc)
(Imm, 20), (rd, 5), (opcode, 7)
Imm: 20-bit immediate value, large, signed-extended
rd: destination operand (where the result should is saved)

J-type (jal)
(Imm_20, 1), (imm_(10:1), 10), (imm_11, 1), (imm_(19:12), 8), (rd, 5), (opcode, 7)
rd: destination operand (where the result should is saved), e.g. return address of jal
Imm needs to be concatenated to form the immediate value, The JAL instruction also uses the PC-relative addressing but the immediate is 20 bits

The target address is called JTA instead of BTA and it is computed as:
JTA = PC+signext(concat(imm20:1, ”0”))
Since the imm-field is 20-bits (with an implicit imm_0), we can jump +/- 2MiB.

Note: The jump register (jr 16(rs1)) does not use PC-relative addressing. It jumps to the memory address contained in register rs1 where the least significant bit is overwritten to '0'. The jr instruction is a pseudoinstruction based on jalr, which jumps to the address pointed by the register plus a given sign-extended immediate value.

ori s0, s1, 0x5A1 -> s0 = s1 | 0x5A1

NOT -> xori t0, s1, 0xffffffff
